title: Two cities
hookLine: we belong to two commonwealths: our town and the whole world (On Leisure 4)
carry: I'm a citizen of the world
last: NOT WISE — LESS BAD EACH DAY.

lines: A BOX WITH ROOM FOR ONE.
cards: Fill in a form and it asks where you're from. A city, a state, a country. A box with room for one answer.
But think about what actually shapes your days: news from the other side of the planet, a cousin in another country, the same moon everyone sees, a sky that doesn't stop at a border.
In the fourth chapter of a short book called On Leisure, Seneca gives the form a second answer, in a single sentence about where you belong.

teach.h: ONE CITY BY BIRTH, ONE BY THE SUN.
teach.b: First, the two. Let's hold in our minds, Seneca writes, two commonwealths.
One is great and truly shared, holding gods and humans alike, where we don't look to this corner or that, but measure our borders by the path of the sun.
The other is the one the accident of birth assigned us: Athens, Carthage, wherever. It belongs to some people, not all. Second, serving both.
Some people serve both cities at once, Seneca says; some only the small one, some only the great one.
His surprise: the great city can be served even in leisure, maybe best in leisure, by thinking clearly about how to live and passing it on. Third, an older echo.

teach.h: DIOGENES: A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Long before Seneca, Diogenes, asked where he came from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world. The Greek word is kosmopolitēs, where we get cosmopolitan.
Seneca's great commonwealth is his own Stoic version of that answer.
Fourth, both, not either. Seneca isn't telling anyone to abandon their town.
You still owe your street, your neighbors, your local school. But you also belong to something with no border, and you owe it something too.
The week, looking back: the raised hand, my faults too, hard training, what does this ask of me, in agreement, less bad each day.
Anger caught, judgment softened, hardship met, faults trimmed: each makes a person easier to share a city with.

how: Some Stoic readers think of themselves as belonging both to their local community and to humanity as a whole, and look for ways to serve each.

o: a life split between city work and country rest
the town you're born in, and the world we all share
two rival cities, like Athens and Carthage

p: assigned by the accident of birth

s: Seneca tells people to abandon their hometown for the world
he says we belong to both, and some serve both at once.
Seneca says the great commonwealth can be served even in leisure
by thinking clearly about how to live and passing it on.
Seneca measures the great commonwealth's borders by the sun's path
not by this corner or that, but as far as the sun runs.

games.q: you're retired from public life. can you still serve the great commonwealth, by Seneca's account?
o: yes, even in leisure, by thinking and passing it on.
games.why: he says the great city can be served in leisure, perhaps even best there.

practice: Picture your small city: your street, the shop on the corner, the people you nod to.

Then let the picture widen to your country, the continent, the whole curve of the planet in sunlight and shadow, people everywhere waking and sleeping. Rest a few breaths in knowing you belong to both.

wordCard.voice: Two cities. Seneca's picture in On Leisure: the town birth gave us, and the great commonwealth measured by the sun. We belong to both. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'citizen of the world': Diogenes' answer, which the Stoics built on.

carryVoice: Your line: I'm a citizen of the world. Your street and the wide world both count. A good week's end.
